blocks.text: Quicksort is a highly efficient sorting algorithm, but what happens when its efficiency degrades? And why can't any comparison-based sort beat $O(n \log n)$?

blocks.markdown: Quicksort is a popular sorting algorithm that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy. It works by selecting a 'pivot' element and partitioning the array into two sub-arrays: elements less than the pivot and elements greater than the pivot. The process is then recursively applied to the sub-arrays.

blocks.title: Partition Step
blocks.text: The partition step in quicksort rearranges the elements in the array such that elements less than the pivot come before it, and elements greater come after it.

blocks.caption: Recurrence relation for Quicksort where $k$ is the number of elements less than the pivot.

blocks.title: Tracing the Partition Step
blocks.prompt: Consider the array [3, 6, 8, 10, 1, 2, 1]. Trace the partition step using 3 as the pivot.

steps.text: Start with the array: [3, 6, 8, 10, 1, 2, 1]. Choose 3 as the pivot.
Rearrange the array to: [1, 2, 1, 3, 6, 8, 10]. Elements less than 3 are on the left, and greater on the right.

blocks.markdown: The choice of pivot is crucial in quicksort. A poor choice can degrade the performance to $O(n^2)$. Ideally, the pivot should split the array into two equal halves.

blocks.title: Worst-case Scenario
blocks.text: Quicksort degrades to $O(n^2)$ when the pivot results in highly unbalanced partitions, such as when the smallest or largest element is always chosen as the pivot.

blocks.title: Pivot Choice Impact
blocks.prompt: Explain how choosing the median as the pivot can improve quicksort's performance.

steps.text: Choosing the median ensures that the array is split into two nearly equal parts.
This results in the recurrence relation $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$, which solves to $O(n \log n)$.

blocks.answer: Choosing the median as the pivot balances the partitions, leading to $O(n \log n)$ complexity.

blocks.markdown: In the context of comparison-based sorting algorithms, there is a fundamental limit to how efficiently they can sort data.

blocks.title: Comparison Sorting Lower Bound
blocks.text: No comparison-based sorting algorithm can have a better average-case complexity than $O(n \log n)$. This is due to the decision tree model of sorting.

blocks.caption: Comparison of sorting algorithms by complexity.

points: Quicksort uses a pivot to partition the array, aiming for balanced sub-arrays.
Poor pivot choice can degrade quicksort to $O(n^2)$.
Comparison-based sorting algorithms cannot surpass $O(n \log n)$ in average-case complexity.
